title: John Locke: Natural Rights and Limited Government

scenes.text: Can a ruler take away your life, liberty, or property?
scenes.narration: Imagine a king claiming he owns everything you have. John Locke said no: your fundamental rights belong to you from birth, not to any ruler!

scenes.text: A housing society committee manages common repairs, but cannot seize your private home.
scenes.narration: Here is an everyday analogy: think of government like a housing society committee. You elect them to fix common lights, not to control your private bedroom.

scenes.heading: Authority: Filmer versus Locke
scenes.narration: Robert Filmer claimed kings inherit God's absolute power over subjects just like fathers rule children. Locke attacked this, showing citizens are rational adults who only obey through consent.

scenes.heading: Locke's Two-Stage Social Contract
scenes.narration: To fix inconveniences where everyone acted as judge, people make two agreements. First, they form a civil society to respect rights; second, they set up an elected government.

scenes.heading: Three Limitations on Property
items: Labour limitation: earn through personal effort
Spoilage limitation: do not waste resources
scenes.narration: Locke defended private property because you mix your own labour with nature. However, he added three limits: work honestly, never waste resources, and leave enough for your neighbours.

scenes.heading: State Power versus People's Rights
scenes.narration: Locke calls government a mere night-watchman trust with limited, delegated powers. Supreme authority stays with the people to protect their natural rights and practice religious toleration.

items: Natural rights to life, liberty, and property
Government is a trust with delegated powers
Right to revolt through peaceful elections
scenes.narration: Remember Locke's big ideas: we own inviolable natural rights, government is only a limited caretaker trust, and citizens can peacefully replace leaders who break faith.
